content.text: Why does a metal spoon heat up faster than water when placed in hot soup? Different substances require different amounts of energy to raise their temperature by the same amount. This property is called specific heat capacity, and understanding it helps us explain many thermal phenomena.

Specific heat capacity (c) tells you how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree C. The equation is E = mc(delta T), where E is energy in joules, m is mass in kg, and delta T is the temperature change.
is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (or 1 K).
Higher c means more energy needed to heat the substance
Lower c means the substance heats up quickly
Specific heat capacity has units of:
(These are equivalent because a change of 1°C equals a change of 1 K)
Specific Heat Capacities of Common Substances

| Substance | c (J/kg·°C) |
|-----------|------------|
| Water | 4200 |
| Ice | 2100 |
| Steam | 2000 |
| Aluminium | 900 |
| Glass | 840 |
| Iron/Steel | 450 |
| Copper | 390 |
| Lead | 130 |
| Oil | 2000 |
| Concrete | 800 |
| Air | 1000 |
Note: Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity compared to most substances.

m_c c_c (T_{initial,c} - T_f) = m_w c_w (T_f - T_{initial,w})

Electrical Method for Measuring c (solid block)

       thermometer
          |
  ========|=========
  ||      |       ||
  ||   [heater]   ||   <-- solid block
  ||              ||
  ===================

  Measure: mass (m), voltage (V), current (I),
           time (t), temperature change (Δθ)
  E = VIt,  c = E / (m × Δθ)
Measure the mass of the block (m)
Heat with electrical heater for time t
Calculate energy: E = P × t = V × I × t
Similar method, but place liquid in an insulated container (calorimeter).

When using E = mc(delta T), remember that delta T is the change in temperature, not the final temperature. If water is heated from 20 degrees C to 80 degrees C, the temperature change is 60 degrees C, not 80 degrees C.
A high specific heat capacity means a substance heats up slowly but also cools down slowly. Water's high SHC (4200 J/(kg degrees C)) is why coastal areas have milder climates than inland areas.
Water has an unusually high c (4200 J/kg·°C) because:
Energy is used to break these bonds, not just increase kinetic energy
Oceans absorb and release large amounts of energy with small temperature changes
Water is an excellent coolant (car radiators, nuclear reactors)
Retain heat for a long time
Coastal areas have milder climates than inland areas
Water is used in central heating because it stores lots of thermal energy
Radiators release heat slowly due to water's high c
Metal pans heat up quickly (low c)
Water-based foods heat slowly but retain heat longer
Release heat during the day (high thermal mass)
Water/coolant absorbs excess heat from engine
Circulates to radiator to release heat
"More mass always means more energy to heat"
— Yes, but specific heat capacity also matters. 1 kg of copper needs less energy than 1 kg of water for the same temperature rise.
"Temperature change tells us how much energy was added"
— Only if we also know mass and specific heat capacity.
"Metal feels cold because it's at a lower temperature"
— Metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your hand quickly, not because it's actually colder.
"All liquids have similar specific heat capacities"
— Water is exceptionally high; oil and alcohol are much lower.
"Heating time is proportional to power only"
— It depends on mass, specific heat capacity, AND power.

Specific heat capacity (c) = energy to raise 1 kg by 1°C
Water has a very high c (4200 J/kg·°C)
Metals have low c (heat quickly but lose heat quickly)
Applications: heating systems, cooling, climate regulation
Measurement: electrical heating method with E = P × t
— Energy lost by iron = energy gained by water. 1 × 450 × (200 − T) = 2 × 4200 × (T − 25). 90,000 − 450T = 8400T − 210,000. 300,000 = 8850T. T = 33.9°C ≈ 34°C (calculation)
Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg·°C).

The sea absorbs large amounts of energy in summer with only a small temperature rise, keeping coastal areas cool. In winter, the sea releases this stored energy slowly, keeping coastal areas warmer. Inland areas lack this moderating effect, so they heat up and cool down more quickly, producing more extreme temperatures. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— m = 1 kg (1 litre of water). E = mcΔθ = 1 × 4200 × 80 = 336,000 J. t = E/P = 336,000/2500 = 134.4 s (calculation)
— At 90% efficiency, useful energy = 0.9 × P × t. So t = E/(0.9 × P) = 336,000/(0.9 × 2500) = 336,000/2250 = 149.3 s (calculation)
